name: Illusion of learning
statement: Study that feels easy is judged to be study that works, so learners rate fluent teaching and rereading above the harder methods that leave them remembering more.
meaning: Two claims sit inside the name. The first is that judgments of learning are built from how the material feels while it is being taken in. Smooth delivery, a second reading and a run of correct answers all raise the sense of knowing, and none of them is a measure of what will survive a week. The second is that the conditions producing durable learning tend to lower that feeling. Bjork and Bjork call those conditions desirable difficulties and list four: varying the conditions of practice, interleaving topics rather than blocking them, spacing rather than massing, and testing rather than presenting. Put the two claims together and the error is systematic rather than random. A learner sampling their own experience will rank the methods in roughly the reverse of the order that a delayed test would give. The word desirable carries weight. A difficulty the learner cannot meet stops helping, which is why this entry is about the calibration of the judgment and not about difficulty as a virtue.

origin.who: Arthur M. Glenberg, Alex Cherry Wilkinson and William Epstein
origin.note: Their paper is "The illusion of knowing: Failure in the self-assessment of comprehension", volume 10, issue 6, pages 597 to 602. Its abstract was read for this entry at Arizona State University's institutional record, and the full text was not obtained. The copy that Unpaywall and OpenAlex both list as open access is a Springer PDF which returns a JavaScript bot challenge rather than the document, tried on 21 September 2026, so the block is a bot challenge and not a paywall. The abstract reports one experiment. It defines the illusion operationally as a reader who failed to find a contradiction in a text and then rated comprehension of that text as high, and it reports illusions more frequent when the contradictory sentences came at the end of three-paragraph texts rather than one-paragraph texts, and when the contradictory information was syntactically marked as new. The study-strategy version of the idea is younger and belongs to Robert Bjork, who dates the term desirable difficulties to a chapter of his in 1994.

evidence: Bjork and Bjork set out the mechanism in a 2011 chapter. Rereading a chapter supplies familiarity and perceptual fluency, which the reader takes for comprehension, and conditions that make performance climb fast during practice are often the ones that fail at a delay. They cite Simon and Bjork's keystroke study, where learners given blocked practice were overconfident about the next day's test. Learners given interleaved practice predicted their own scores closely. They also cite Rohrer and Taylor on volume formulas, at 63% correct a week later after interleaved instruction against 20% after blocked. Both figures are quoted here from that chapter and not from the papers. Kornell and Bjork measured the gap directly. In Experiment 1a, 120 UCLA undergraduates saw 72 paintings, six by each of 12 artists, for 3 seconds apiece, with half the artists massed and half interleaved, then identified the painter of new works. On the first test block, spaced study gave .61 correct against .35, t(119) = 10.82, d = 0.99, and Experiment 1b reproduced it between subjects with 72 participants at .59 against .36, t(70) = 4.94, d = 1.28. Then the questionnaire. Of the 120, 78% had done better in the spaced condition and 78% said massing had been as good as spacing or better. A style-recognition version with 80 participants gave hits of .77 against .67, t(79) = 3.28, d = 0.41, and of the 72 who expressed a preference, 64 picked massing. Asked afterwards which artists had been massed, 28 participants named the schedule above chance for spaced artists, .74, t(27) = 7.48, p < .0001, and not for massed ones, .55, t(27) = 1.19, p = .25. Each of those is a test against chance rather than a comparison of the two. The judgment was not a memory of the schedule. It was a reading of how study had felt. Carpenter, Wilford, Kornell and Mullaney moved the cue to the teacher. Forty-two Iowa State undergraduates watched one of two 65-second videos of the same speaker explaining why calico cats are usually female, upright and without notes or hunched over a podium reading haltingly. Predicted recall was higher after the fluent version, t(40) = 3.34, p = .002, d = 1.03. Actual recall of the 10 idea units did not differ, t < 0.50. Overconfidence ran at .22 against .03, t(40) = 3.02, p = .004, d = 0.93. In a second experiment with 70 students, test scores were .44 against .40, t(68) = 0.81, p = .42, and time spent studying the script afterwards was 1.39 minutes against 1.43. One participant in the first experiment and four in the second were replaced for reporting prior knowledge of the topic. Deslauriers, McCarty, Miller, Callaghan and Kestin ran the classroom version. In two semesters of calculus-based introductory physics at Harvard, 149 of 157 students were randomly split for two 90-minute meetings in week 12, one on static equilibrium and one on fluids. Both rooms got identical slides, handouts and worked solutions from instructors trained in both styles; the only variable was whether students attempted the problems in small groups first or were told how to solve them. Each class ended with a feeling-of-learning survey and a 12-question test written by an author who had not seen the materials. Students in the active rooms scored 0.46 standard deviations higher on the test and reported 0.56 standard deviations lower feeling of learning, both P < 0.001. The models controlled for prior physics knowledge, attitudes, two earlier midterms and gender. Adding perceived teaching effectiveness to the model absorbed the effect: that rating predicted feeling of learning at 0.51, P < 0.001, and active against passive stopped predicting it. Seventeen students interviewed afterwards described the active classes as disjointed and lacking flow, 15 of 17, and all but one found the passive lecture easier to follow.

examples.text: Rereading a chapter makes it smooth on the page, and the smoothness is taken as a sign it has gone in. A week later the reader who shut the book and tried to write the argument out from memory has more of it.

A polished lecture, well paced and cleanly delivered, leaves an audience confident it understood. A muddier session that made them work the steps out leaves them less confident and better able to do the problems.
A student blocks each subject into its own week, because a week of one thing feels like progress. Mixing the subjects makes every session feel worse and leaves more standing at the exam.

replication.headline: The strategy version reproduces. The classroom version has gone both ways: Boedeker's crossover trial with 146 medical students found feeling of learning 0.56 standard deviations higher in the active session, the same size as Deslauriers's gap and the opposite sign.
replication.detail: Boedeker and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine copied the design and credit Deslauriers for it. Of 181 students in the second-year course, 146 consented and sat both sessions, randomised across two days of 50-minute classes, hypertension on one day and electrocardiogram interpretation on the other. Each student took one session as a lecture and one as a large-group interactive class, on the same clinical vignettes and the same slides. Three faculty members who had not seen the lesson materials wrote a 12-question test for each topic, and each session ended with a feeling-of-learning survey and that test. Learners scored 0.27 standard deviations higher after the interactive session, 95% CI [0.07, 0.47], p = 0.010. Their feeling of learning was 0.56 standard deviations higher, 95% CI [0.36, 0.76], p < 0.001, with all four survey items pointing the same way on both days. The authors attribute the reversal to the stage of learner, since their participants held degrees and a year of medical school. A second classroom attempt runs back the other way. Lee, Wages and Nam compared active against passive teaching in developmental and introductory psychology classes over two semesters, and report exam scores rising in the active group while that group felt it had learned less, which is the Harvard pattern. Their article carries no DOI at Crossref and only the abstract at the journal's own site was read here, so no figure from it is quoted. The instructor-fluency leg is unsettled inside the laboratory that found it. Carpenter, Mickes, Rahman and Fernandez repeated the manipulation with a 22-minute lecture and tested at three delays. The fluent instructor was rated higher on organisation, knowledge, preparedness and effectiveness in all three experiments, with d from .53 to 1.26. Judgments of learning did not follow: 62% against 62%, t(68) = .05, then 44% against 48%, t(100) = .99, p = .33, then 63% against 57%, t(89) = 1.55, p = .12. Test scores were 66% against 65%, then 56% against 62%, then 60% against 52%, t(89) = 2.07, p = .041, d = .43. Carpenter, Northern, Tauber and Toftness then ran two experiments on a 30-minute information-theory lecture, telling half of each group that the instructor was experienced. Fluency raised judgments of learning both times, F(1, 186) = 24.05, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.11 on the 190 analysed of 194 recruited, and F(1, 173) = 33.60, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.16 on the 177 analysed of 191, after 14 were dropped for misreporting how experienced the instructor was. Test scores moved neither time, F(1, 186) = 2.13, p = .15 and F(1, 173) = 1.14, p = .29, and the experience manipulation moved neither measure. Those figures come from the advance online version of that paper, posted in 2019 on the first author's own site, not from the 2020 issue.

study.cite: Boedeker, P., Schlingmann, T., Kailin, J., Nair, A., Foldes, C., Rowley, D., Salciccioli, K., Maag, R., Moreno, N., & Ismail, N. (2024). Active versus passive learning in large-group sessions in medical school: A randomized cross-over trial investigating effects on learning and the feeling of learning. Medical Science Educator, 35(1), 459-467.

limits: The two classroom studies do not measure the same thing, and the coincidence of 0.56 hides it. Deslauriers's composite came from four items about perceived learning, and he kept the rating of teaching effectiveness out of it, using that rating instead as the thing that explained the gap. Boedeker's adapted composite also has four items: enjoyment of the session, feeling one learned a great deal, a rating of how effective the instructor was, and a wish that all courses were taught that way. The item the two share is the second. Deslauriers's other three sit in a figure and a supplementary appendix, neither of which was read here. A student who liked the class, or liked the teacher, registers in Boedeker's composite as a student who felt they learned. Deslauriers's test was 12 multiple-choice questions; Boedeker's was 12 questions whose format the paper does not give. Both were taken in the room minutes after the teaching, so neither speaks to retention. Deslauriers's design also moved both groups away from their normal class, which usually mixed lecturing with occasional activities, and the passive lecture was built to maximise fluency of delivery. The intervention at the end of that paper is self-report from a later course, with over 65% of students reporting that their feelings about the effectiveness of active learning improved across the semester and 75% saying the start-of-term intervention helped, and no control group. Kornell and Bjork's participants were UCLA undergraduates sorting paintings by unfamiliar artists, and Carpenter's watched a 65-second video about cats; how far either travels to a syllabus is untested there. No multi-site or registered replication of any of these results was located in a search on 21 September 2026 of Crossref by title and by DOI, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and general web search under "feeling of learning", "illusion of knowing", "instructor fluency" and "judgments of learning". Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell's 2013 Annual Review survey is closed at Annual Reviews and Unpaywall records no repository copy, but the authors' accepted manuscript sits on the Bjork lab's own page at UCLA and was read there. It is not the typeset article, so the page range in the citation comes from Crossref and not from the document read. In that manuscript Kornell and Bjork report surveying 472 UCLA undergraduates, 76% of whom said they reread whole chapters or their own underlining.
misreadings: The finding is not that students dislike learning or that discomfort is the active ingredient. Bjork and Bjork's word is desirable, and a difficulty beyond what the learner can meet is on their account an undesirable one. This atlas records both halves of that. Entry 98 notes that retrieval which mostly fails buys nothing, and entry 20 records that setting a problem in hard-to-read type failed to improve reasoning in a large multi-site replication. Difficulty is a by-product of the useful conditions, not the mechanism. A second error is to read the feeling as uninformative. In Carpenter's three-experiment follow-up the correlation between students' judgments and their test scores was positive every time, from r = .30 to r = .44. The judgment is biased by a cue, which is a different claim from the judgment being noise. A third is to treat this as the Dunning-Kruger effect in a classroom. Deslauriers adds a moderately significant interaction, P < 0.05, between prior physics knowledge and feeling of learning, with students who knew more physics showing a more positive link between feeling and performance. The driver measured in these studies is the fluency of the material and its delivery, not the learner's skill. The fourth is the one that gets quoted from the Harvard paper. Its 0.46 standard deviations is a within-class result on a 12-item quiz taken at the end of a single 90-minute meeting, not a course grade and not a delayed measure. The broader claim that active learning outperforms lecturing rests on Freeman and colleagues' meta-analysis of 225 studies. It put examination and concept-inventory performance 0.47 standard deviations higher across 158 studies, Z = 9.781, and the odds of failing at 1.95 under traditional lecturing across 67, Z = 10.4, with average failure rates of 21.8% under active learning against 33.8% under lecturing. That is the evidence for the learning half. Deslauriers's contribution is the feeling half. The last error is to assume the illusion lifts once a learner is shown the evidence. Yan, Bjork and Bjork ran six experiments on Kornell and Bjork's painting task. In their sixth, 197 people were recruited on Mechanical Turk and 155 analysed; interleaved study beat blocked study, .74 against .64, F(1, 153) = 35.59, p < .001, partial eta squared .19. Told nothing, 46% of that group still judged interleaving the better schedule against 37% for blocking. Only when the two schedules were separated into different study and test phases and the reason for the illusion was explained did the figure reach 75%. In their third, fourth and fifth experiments, where the schedules were intermixed, the share preferring interleaving never passed 50%. Their method section and their results section disagree over which of the two groups in the sixth experiment held 76 people and which held 79, so the percentages above are quoted without denominators.
